headline: TRAI Drive Test: Reliance Jio Leads Mobile Network Performance in Himachal Pradesh, Airtel Achieves 209.58 Mbps on Highway
content: Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel have demonstrated superior mobile network performance in Himachal Pradesh, outperforming Vodafone Idea and BSNL in download speeds, upload speeds and network coverage across Una, Mandi, Joginder Nagar and major highway routes, according to the latest drive test findings released by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI). Reliance Jio achieved the highest download speed of 171.68 Mbps across city routes, while Airtel recorded the highest download speed of 209.58 Mbps on the Mandi–Una highway. BSNL and Vodafone Idea continued to face significant network coverage gaps and relatively high call drop rates. TRAI conducted drive test between September 15 and September 18, 2026, covering 373 km of city routes, 225.1 km of highway routes, 5.2 km of pedestrian routes, six hotspot locations and one inter-operator calling test location. Reliance Jio leads mobile network performance across city routes Reliance Jio recorded the highest 5G download speed of 171.68 Mbps across Una, Mandi and Joginder Nagar, followed by Airtel at 122.28 Mbps. Vodafone Idea achieved 4G download speed of 12.18 Mbps, while BSNL recorded 9.49 Mbps. Reliance Jio’s download speed was approximately 40.4 percent higher than Airtel, 14.1 times faster than Vodafone Idea and 18.1 times faster than BSNL.

headline: National tribute to Sardar Sobha Singh; Centre notifies Rs 125 commemorative coin
content: In a landmark recognition of Indian art, the Government of India has notified the issuance of a Rs 125 commemorative coin in honour of legendary painter Sobha Singh on his 125th birth anniversary. The notification was issued in the Gazette of India on November 25, making him the first Indian painter to be honoured with a commemorative coin in his memory. The coin will likely be released in February next year.The announcement has brought national recognition to the celebrated artist whose life and work connected Punjab and Himachal Pradesh, particularly Andretta in Kangra district, which he made his home after Partition in 1947.The coin will be released as part of year-long celebrations marking his 125th birth anniversary, from November 2026 to November 2027, under the theme 'Janambhoomi Se Karmabhoomi Tak'.Expressing gratitude to the Centre, KG Butail, president of the Sobha Singh Memorial Art Society, Andretta, said the notification was the culmination of sustained efforts to secure national recognition for the legendary painter."It is a moment of immense pride not only for the people of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab but also for the entire Indian art fraternity. Sobha Singh's contribution to Indian art and his humanistic philosophy deserved recognition at the national level. The commemorative coin will ensure that his legacy reaches generations to come," he said.Butail acknowledged the support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Union Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat in taking the proposal forward. He also expressed gratitude to former Union ministers Anurag Thakur and Vijay Sampla, former Himachal Chief Minister Shanta Kumar and former Rajya Sabha MP Tarlochan Singh for their efforts in pursuing the demand.Dr Hirday Paul Singh, secretary general of the Society and grandson of the artist, described the development as an emotionally significant moment for the family and admirers of Sobha Singh across the world."The commemorative coin is a fitting and enduring tribute to an artist whose work transcended geographical, religious and social boundaries. His paintings conveyed a universal message of humanity and compassion. This recognition will take his life, philosophy and artistic legacy to a much wider national and international audience," he said.Born on November 29, 1901, at Sri Hargobindpur in Punjab, Sobha Singh made Andretta his “karmabhoomi” after Partition in 1947. His iconic portraits of Sikh Gurus, historical personalities and spiritual figures earned him widespread acclaim. His paintings, particularly those depicting Sikh Gurus, remain an enduring part of India's artistic and cultural heritage.The Society said the commemorative coin would be more than a birth anniversary memento, serving as a lasting national tribute to the artist's contribution to Indian art and culture.

headline: Treat Agnipath 1.0 & 2.0 as pilot projects. India needs Agnipath 3.0
content: On 4 November, the government announced a major revision of the Agnipath scheme, introduced in 2022 for short-term recruitment of soldiers into the armed forces. Under the revised arrangement, 25 per cent of Agniveers completing their initial four-year engagement will be selected for regular service. The remaining 75 per cent will be offered another two years of engagement. At the end of six years, they will also be eligible for regular enrolment, subject to their willingness and the prescribed selection criteria. The extended engagement comes with higher remuneration and an enhanced Seva Nidhi package. Those regularised after six years will rank below the 25 per cent regularised after four years in seniority. The armed forces have described the revision as the outcome of an assessment of Agniveers’ performance and organisational requirements. While Agnipath 2.0 does address the organisational need to retain trained manpower, it jettisons the lofty goals of a younger profile for soldiers and a reduced pension bill. It also miserably fails to address the problem of “unequal soldiers”, which affects the morale, cohesion and ethos of the armed forces. The move also comes in the wake of Gen Z protests in July and October and ahead of crucial elections next year in UP, Punjab, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, which together contribute 32.58 per cent of soldiers to the armed forces. The original Agnipath scheme was conceived to address two genuine structural challenges: rising pension expenditure, which constrains transformation, and the ageing profile of the armed forces. India does need a more economical and younger military, but not at the cost of professional effectiveness, soldierly motivation and fairness. Agnipath 2.0 has modified the terms of engagement without resolving these contradictions. It is a virtual restoration of the status quo ante after 4-6 years of unethical exploitation of Agniveers as “unequal soldiers”. There are also reports citing “senior officials” as saying that the new framework “will apply only to existing Agniveers” and that the scheme is “expected to undergo further changes for recruits inducted into the three services after 31 December.” It is empirical wisdom that large militaries can only be sustained by a viable short-term engagement system which meets organisational and individual needs. All modern militaries follow this system. I propose an Agnipath 3.0 based on a modernised Colour-Reserve system combining short-term engagement, differentiated retention as regular soldiers, a trained reserve and assured resettlement. India is not experimenting with short-term military engagement for the first time.

headline: Delhi University's Samten Choedon wins Academic Gold Medal, inspiring Tibetan refugee students with her j
content: Samten Choedon has been awarded the University Gold Medal by the University of Delhi (DU) for topping the Master of Arts (MA) programme in East Asian Studies, with a cumulative grade point average (CGPA) of 9.063, according to tibet.net, the website of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). She received the medal on November 20, 2026.tibet.net describes the moment as overwhelming and emotional for her, and as the result of years of hard work and perseverance.From Arunachal Pradesh to Dharamshala to DelhiSamten was born in Arunachal Pradesh and raised in Dharamshala, Himachal Pradesh. She completed her schooling at Tibetan Children’s Villages (TCV) Suja and TCV Gopalpur, tibet.net reports.She then did a Bachelor of Arts (BA) Honours in Political Science at Miranda House, University of Delhi, followed by her MA in East Asian Studies at the same university.Why East Asian StudiesHer interest in politics, history and international relations led her to the subject. She wanted to understand China and the changing geopolitical dynamics of Asia, and she also wanted to examine Tibet within the wider context of Chinese politics and history.According to tibet.net, she often brought Tibetan perspectives into her academic research. That is not a small point in a field where Tibet is usually a footnote to a larger China story.The postgraduate adjustmentSamten said adapting to the research-oriented demands of postgraduate studies was difficult. Through consistent effort and guidance, she gradually built her research and writing skills, tibet.net reports.Now, toppers’ advice usually sounds like a poster slogan. Hers is more specific. She credits her result to staying consistent, understanding concepts and being willing to learn from her mistakes.Support from the Department of EducationSamten said she is grateful for the scholarships and educational support she received from the Department of Education, CTA. She believes the support gave her financial assistance, and also confidence and motivation through her studies, according to tibet.net.What comes nextShe hopes to pursue further studies, possibly a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in China, East Asian politics or International Relations. She also plans to keep contributing to the Tibetan community as much as she can, tibet.net says.Her message to young Tibetans is to believe in themselves and not underestimate their abilities. She asks them to treat education as a privilege and an opportunity, and reminds them that they are equally capable of excellence.The dedicationSamten has dedicated the medal to the 14th Dalai Lama and to her parents, whose vision, sacrifices, encouragement and support, she says, made her journey possible.For her, tibet.net writes, the Gold Medal is not only an individual accomplishment but “a reflection of the support and opportunities that have shaped her life.” The Department of Education, CTA, congratulated her and wished her success in her future work.Get the latest Education News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: DA hike: Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Tripura, Gujarat, Kerala — check full list of states with second increase
content: DA hike update: The Union Cabinet hiked dearness allowance by 3% for central government employees and pensioners, raising the component from 60% to 63% of basic pay, effective from 1 July.This was the second DA increase this year, after the Centre hiked the component by 2% in April from 58% to 60%, effective from 1 January and is in line with the 7th central pay commission (CPC) recommendation that DA be revised twice annually, using data from the All-India Consumer Price Index (AICPI).DA is a percentage of employees' basic pay that aims to mitigate the impact of the rising cost of living and inflation. Usually, announcements from the Centre come in March and October, with rollouts in January and July. Over 1 crore beneficiaries — about 50 lakh central government employees and nearly 65 lakh pensioners, including defence and railway personnel and retirees gain from DA and dearness relief (DR) hikes.Full list of states which announced second DA hikeBesides the Finance Ministry's announcement on 28 October, state governments also hiked DA for employees and pensioners ahead of Diwali.This includes a 5% hike by the Himachal Pradesh government, 4% DA hike by Mizoram, 3% DA hikes each by the Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Tripura, Odisha and Gujarat governments, 2.5% increase by the Karnataka government, and 2% increases by the Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Kerala governments.Tripura enhanced dearness allowance and dearness relief (DR) for state government employees and pensioners by 3% in October, to 44% of basic salary — an increase of 8% this year and 36% since 2022, according to Chief Minister Manik Saha.The Jharkhand state government in November hiked DA and DR by 3% each from 60% to 63%, effective from 1 July and benefitting around 3 lakh state government employees and pensioners.Karnataka on 5 November hiked DA and DR for state government employees and pensioners drawing salaries under the 2024 Revised Pay Scales by 2.5%, from 15.75% to 18%, with effect from 1 July 2026, PTI reported.Arunachal Pradesh increased DA and DR for state government employees and pensioners by three percentage points, from 60% to 63%, effective from 1 July. The enhanced DA and DR will also benefit central and state All India Services (AIS) officers on deputation to the state. CM Pema Khandu said that arrears for the four-month period from July to October will be paid in cash and credited directly to beneficiary accounts.Uttar Pradesh increased DA by 3%, from 60% of basic pay to 63%, with effect from 1 July 2026. The hike will be implemented for lakhs of state government employees, staff in aided educational and technical institutions, regular and full-time employees of urban local bodies, work-charged employees, and those serving on University Grants Commission (UGC) pay scales. DA for October will be paid along with regular salary for November.Bihar hiked DA and DR for state government employees and pensioners covered under the 5th, 6th and 7th Central Pay Commissions (CPCs), with effect from 1 July, as follows — under the 7th CPC up 3%, from 60% to 63%; under 6th CPC up 7% from 262% to 269%; and under 5th CPC, up 14% from 483% to 497%.Uttarakhand approved a 3% DA hike for state government employees, increasing the component to 63% of basic pay, with effect from 1 July 2026. Beneficiaries include the state government employees, eligible personnel working in local bodies, aided educational institutions, state universities, technical educational institutions, and those drawing salaries under the University Grants Commission (UGC) pay scales. DA arrears for 1 July to 31 October 2026, will be paid in cash to eligible employees.The Mizoram state government also announced a four% hike in DA this month for its employees, raising it from 46% to 50% with effect from December 1. Further, the state cabinet approved doubling DA for contractual employees from 10% to 20%, effective December 1.Odisha has hiked DA and DR for state employees and pensioners, respectively, by 3%, increased from 60% to 63%, coming into effect retrospectively from July 1, Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi announced this month. Around 8.5 lakh Odisha government employees and pensioners will benefit from the raise to be paid in cash along with November salary, as per a statement from the CMO.Tamil Nadu on 31 October announced a 3% DA hike, from the existing 60% rate to 63% for state government employees, teachers and pensioners. Benefiting around 16 lakh state government employees, teachers, pensioners, and family pensioners, the increase will be effective from 1 July 2026.Rajasthan on 30 October approved a 3% increase in DA and DR for state employees and pensioners to 63% of basic pay. Over 7 lakh government employees and over 5 lakh pensioners will benefit from the revision, effective from 1 July 2026 and to be paid in the November and December salaries, respectively, while arrears for the four-month period from July to October will be deposited in their General Provident Fund (GPF) accounts.Also on 30 October, Madhya Pradesh announced a 2% DA hike for state government employees, including officers and pensioners, ahead of Diwali, with effect from 1 January. CM Mohan Yadav said arrears for nine months, from January to September, will be paid in three equal monthly instalments. From October, the increased DA will be paid in cash with salaries (October's DA payable in November salary). Meanwhile, DR will be effective from July.The Chhattisgarh government on 29 October hiked DA by 2%, taking it to 60% of basic pay from the existing 58%, with effect from 1 November. “The decision will benefit around 3.85 lakh state government employees and 1.5 lakh pensioners,” CM Vishnu Deo Sai said.Earlier in the month, Himachal Pradesh increased DA by 5%, from 45% to 50%, for eligible state government employees covered by the Himachal Pradesh Civil Services (Revised Pay) Rules, 2022, All India Services officers and state government employees covered by UGC pay scales. The additional DA will be paid in cash with the October 2026 salary, payable in November 2026.Kerala hiked DA and DR by 2% from 35% to 37%, to be paid with the October 2026 salary, disbursed in November, for state government employees, teachers, full-time contingent employees and local government staff, state service pensioners, family pensioners, and eligible ex-gratia pensioners and their families.

headline: 91 Medicine Samples Manufactured in Himachal Fail Quality Tests; Solan Accounts for 65 Cases
content: Shimla: In a major setback to Himachal Pradesh’s pharmaceutical industry, as many as 91 medicine samples manufactured in the state have failed to meet prescribed quality standards during recent testing. Across the country, a total of 324 medicine samples have been declared substandard. Of the 91 failed samples from Himachal Pradesh, the highest number came from Solan district, which accounted for 65 cases. Sirmaur recorded 19 failed samples, followed by five from Una and two from Kangra. The medicines that failed quality tests belong to several therapeutic categories and are used to treat a range of health conditions, including infections, anaemia, itching, fever, cough and cold, pain, acidity, diabetes, high blood pressure, asthma and high cholesterol. The findings have once again raised concerns over the quality of medicines manufactured in the state’s pharmaceutical hubs, particularly in the industrial belt of Solan and adjoining areas. State Drug Controller Dr Manish Kapoor said the department would initiate action against the pharmaceutical companies concerned under the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Notices will be issued to the manufacturers, directing them to recall the affected batches of medicines from the market. The department will also take necessary action in accordance with the applicable legal provisions.

headline: Himachal to get 50% free power royalty from central PSUs after 40 years of project operation, says CM
content: Himachal Pradesh government has approved an amendment to Swaran Jayanti Energy Policy-2021 to enhance free power royalty from hydroelectric projects operated by Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), including the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam (SJVN) and National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), upon completion of 40 years of commissioning.According to the amended provisions, these projects will be required to provide free power royalty to the state at the enhanced rate of 50% for the first 10 years after completing 40 years of operation. Thereafter, on completion of 50 years of operation, the projects will revert to the state government free of cost and without any encumbrances or liabilities. Separate agreements will be executed with the concerned CPSUs to give effect to these provisions.At present, the state receives free power royalty under the existing policy at the rate of 12% for the first 12 years, 18% for the subsequent 18 years and 30% for the remaining 10 years of the agreement period. However, the provisions notified on September 30, 2024, primarily covered projects allotted or proposed to be allotted to central and state PSUs and joint-sector entities and did not address the enhancement of royalty from existing projects operated by NHPC, SJVN and NTPC.The amendment will cover several major hydroelectric projects in the state, including Baira Siul, Chamera-I, Chamera-II, Chamera-III, Parbati Stage-II and Parbati Stage-III operated by NHPC, Nathpa Jhakri and Rampur projects operated by SJVN and Kol Dam operated by NTPC. Notably, the Baira Suil Hydroelectric Project, commissioned in 1982, has already completed more than 40 years of commercial operation.The Himachal Pradesh government maintains that water is among the most valuable natural resources of the state, particularly in view of its unique geographical and economic circumstances as a hill state.“The amendment seeks to ensure that the state receives a fairer and enhanced share of the benefits generated through the utilisation of its water resources, especially from hydroelectric projects that have completed 40 years of operation,” a government official spokesperson said.Chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu said the state government was firmly committed to protecting the interests of Himachal Pradesh and ensuring that its natural resources were utilised in a manner that maximises benefits for its people. “Hydropower was one of the major sources of revenue for the state, and it was essential to ensure that Himachal Pradesh received its rightful share from projects harnessing its water resources,” he said.The chief minister said that the enhanced free power royalty would strengthen the state’s financial position and generate additional resources for developmental and welfare activities.

headline: In Himachal’s Chamba, Damaged Homes Expose Risks of Roads and Poor Drainage
content: Chamba, Himachal Pradesh: Seventy-five-year-old Rana Pratap remembers the night of August 27, when heavy rain sent water, stones and debris rushing towards his house in Obdi village in Himachal Pradesh's Chamba district.Around midnight, he heard stones falling and being swept away by the rushing water. A road runs above his house, and soon rainwater from the road began flowing towards it. Realising the danger, Pratap woke his family and moved them to safety.“I have two sons and the whole family was at home. We could have all been finished that night. By God's grace, we survived,” he told 101Reporters.Moments later, a hillside collapse sent large rocks crashing onto the house.For Pratap's family, escaping the disaster was only the beginning. Their house was completely damaged, forcing them to move into rented accommodation. His son Raj Kumar's house was also damaged..The incident was part of a difficult monsoon for Chamba, where heavy rainfall and flash floods damaged homes, roads and public infrastructure. On July 28, torrential rain and flash runoff carrying boulders, mud and silt inundated residential and commercial neighbourhoods in Chamba town and adjoining areas.In July, the district recorded 447.5 mm of rainfall against the monthly normal of 305.7 mm, marking a 46% excess. Between June and September, however, Chamba received 785.4 mm of rainfall, around 8% below its seasonal normal.The uneven distribution of rainfall, with a particularly wet July followed by below-normal rainfall in August and September, highlights how seasonal totals can obscure the intensity of individual rainfall events.The damage has also raised questions about how roads, drainage systems and settlements interact in the district's mountainous terrain, and whether inadequate drainage can increase the vulnerability of homes during heavy rainfall..See Also: Supreme Court judgement ends the decades old Bhakra-Nangal and Beas hydroelectricity dispute; issues relief for Himachal Pradesh.How roads can increase the riskIn mountainous areas, roads can alter the natural movement of rainwater. Road construction can intercept runoff flowing down slopes and concentrate it along roadside drains and culverts. If these structures are blocked, inadequately designed or poorly positioned, water can be diverted towards houses and settlements, erode slopes and contribute to flooding.In Obdi, residents allege that changes to the drainage arrangement along the road above their houses worsened the situation.For 47-year-old Ramesh Kumar, a taxi driver, the problem had begun before the disaster. He says rainwater previously passed beneath the road through a cross-drainage structure. However, he alleges that the existing water passage was blocked by a concrete wall.Ramesh says he repeatedly approached the Public Works Department's Chamba Division-II, asking officials to construct a drain behind the road or provide a culvert to divert water away from the houses below.He also raised concerns about the road's slope and the positioning of the drainage works, saying they could direct rainwater towards the residential area.“I told both the contractor and the JE that they should not do the work this way. I warned them that if the water was diverted towards our houses, it could put our families and property in danger. But no one listened to us. They completed the work and left, and now we are the ones paying the price,” he said.Ramesh alleges that the concrete wall was constructed before the necessary drainage arrangements were completed. He says crate work has only recently begun.The allegations have not been independently established. An assessment of the site and its drainage design would be necessary to determine whether the road works contributed to the damage.Kanav Badotra, executive engineer of the Public Works Department's Chamba-II division, told 101Reporters that the road was a panchayat road, with approximately two kilometres falling under the department's jurisdiction for maintenance and repair.Addressing the risks posed by runoff, Badotra said the location of such incidents was difficult to predict and that water flowing down a slope could exert enough force to destabilise the ground and trigger a disaster. He added that the department could undertake only those works for which funds were available.The department's response does not establish whether the drainage arrangement in Obdi was adequate or whether the concerns raised by residents were investigated.A new policy for road drainageRepeated monsoon damage has prompted the Himachal Pradesh government to introduce measures aimed at improving road drainage and protecting vulnerable mountain slopes.The state notified its Road Drainage Policy on February 19, 2026, citing the particularly destructive monsoons of 2023 and 2025. The policy seeks to improve how roads are designed and maintained in relation to local terrain and rainfall conditions.It emphasises drainage systems suited to the surrounding landscape, adequately designed culverts and arrangements to ensure that rainwater is safely channelled rather than discharged towards vulnerable slopes and settlements.Separate guidelines for road drainage improvement works, notified in July 2026, provide for better-designed roadside drains and improvements across longer stretches of roads.The state has also outlined a separate approach to slope protection and stabilisation, addressing risks such as landslides, soil erosion and falling rocks.Ashok Kumar Thakur, a junior engineer with the State National Highway Division in Chamba, told 101Reporters that the policy was a necessary step given Himachal Pradesh's terrain and rainfall conditions.“In hilly areas, road drainage is not just about constructing drains alongside roads. It also requires understanding the natural flow of water, ensuring that culverts have adequate capacity, and making sure that rainwater runoff does not create problems for slopes or nearby settlements,” he said.However, improving drainage along newly constructed roads addresses only part of the problem. Existing roads and settlements may already have altered natural drainage patterns, making it necessary to assess and repair infrastructure that was built without adequate consideration of water flow.The distinction is particularly important in Chamba, where settlements have developed over decades around valleys and natural drainage channels.Kulbhushan Upmanyu, an environmentalist, said that simply moving people away from such locations was not always practical. The challenge, he said, was to ensure that construction and development took account of the natural movement of water.Where a stream or natural drainage channel has historically carried large volumes of water, rocks and debris during the monsoon, ignoring that pattern can put homes, roads and residents at risk.The problem also extends to new construction. While existing settlements may require better drainage and protective measures, new roads and buildings need to account for natural water channels and slope stability before construction begins.The new policies seek to address some of these concerns, but their effectiveness will depend on how they are implemented and whether existing infrastructure is included in the improvements.Arun Singh, a civil engineer from Shimla, said proper drainage was essential for the safety and long-term stability of roads in a mountainous state such as Himachal Pradesh.He said drains could become blocked with silt and debris during heavy rainfall, while culverts with inadequate capacity might struggle to carry runoff. If water was not channelled safely, it could erode slopes and affect nearby houses and settlements.Singh said the new policy was a useful step because it emphasised planned drainage systems, appropriately designed culverts, paved shoulders and the safe disposal of rainwater.However, he said the engineering solutions needed to be suited to local conditions and accompanied by regular maintenance.“Every road stretch has different terrain and drainage requirements. The system must be designed accordingly to ensure that water is not simply diverted from the road towards another vulnerable area,” he said.The implementation of the policies also raises questions about the coverage of existing rural roads. While the Slope Protection and Stabilisation Policy includes rural, link and panchayat roads, the first phase of the Road Drainage Improvement Guidelines restricts proposals under its dedicated budget head to Major District Roads.This leaves questions about how drainage problems along smaller roads will be addressed and which agencies will be responsible for the necessary improvements..See Also: Nearly a year after Himachal's monsoon disaster, Beru village is still waiting for relief.Years of savings buried under debrisFor the families in Obdi, the immediate challenge is rebuilding their homes and recovering from their losses.Ramesh's elder brother, 49-year-old Raj Kumar, says 11 people lived in the two houses affected by the disaster. He estimates that he spent around Rs 15 lakh-Rs 17 lakh building his house over several years of work as a driver.Household belongings, utensils and appliances, including a scooter and refrigerator, were damaged.“We had built this house with a lot of hard work and sweat. I am a driver, and whatever I earned, I put into building the house. Seeing everything damaged is painful. It is not easy for us to build everything again,” he said.Ramesh estimates that he spent nearly Rs 20 lakh building his house.In Gholti, 29-year-old Vivek Kumar also lost his rented accommodation and household belongings. He had moved there from Larkha village in the Bharmour Assembly constituency in search of work and was doing daily-wage jobs.A day before the disaster, Vivek moved to a neighbour's house with his wife and two-year-old daughter after stones began falling near their rented room.He estimated that household items worth around Rs 5 lakh, including a bed box, sofa, cupboard, television and washing machine, were buried under the debris. His wife's gold ring and earrings were also lost, he said.Following the incident, the administration arranged for families whose houses were completely damaged to move into rented accommodation.A report submitted by the Tehsildar, Sadar Chamba, to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate recorded that Rana Pratap, Raj Kumar and Vivek Kumar had shifted to rented houses. Their monthly rents were recorded as Rs 4,000, Rs 5,000 and Rs 4,000, respectively..Ravi Bhardwaj, pradhan of Draman panchayat, told 101Reporters that the panchayat had prepared the necessary documents for the affected families and forwarded them to the SDM's office for further processing.He said the families had also received financial assistance, clothes and essential items from some non-governmental organisations in the immediate aftermath of the disaster.The affected families were told during a visit by local MLA Neeraj Nayar that they would receive around Rs 7 lakh in government assistance, Bhardwaj said.According to information from the SDM's office, the compensation files have been forwarded for further processing. However, the families say they are still waiting for the assistance and have had to meet their immediate expenses through their own earnings.Ramesh said he had also hired labourers at his own expense to clear the debris from the damaged property.For the families, rebuilding their homes remains a distant prospect. The immediate relief arrangements have provided temporary accommodation, but they are still waiting for compensation to help them recover their losses.101Reporters also sought information from the Chamba Deputy Commissioner's office regarding the flood damage. Emails sent on September 11 and September 22, followed by a phone call to the Disaster Management Cell, did not receive a response.[Wc/HP].Suggested Reading:.Uttarakhand’s Chir Pine Forests Generate Crores in Revenue, but Local Communities See Few Benefits.Subscribe to our channels on YouTube and WhatsAppDownload our app on Play Store

headline: Dogra Degree College bags ICF Award for achievement in academic activities
content: Excelsior CorrespondentJAMMU, Nov 25: Dogra Degree College, Bari Brahmana, a constituent of the Dogra Group of Colleges under Dogra Educational Trust, has been honoured with the Indian Colleges Forum (ICF) recognition and award for achievement in academic activities.Dr Samar Dev Singh Charak, secretary, Dogra Educational Trust, received the award on behalf of the college at the valedictory session and award ceremony of the 27th National Annual Conference of ICF, held recently at GGDSD College, Rajpur, Palampur, district Kangra, Himachal Pradesh.The three-day conference, organized by ICF and the Society for Education and Economic Development (SEED) in collaboration with GGDSD College, was held on the theme "Higher Education in the Era of Industry 6.0". The inaugural session was graced by Prof Lalit Kumar Awasthi, Vice-Chancellor, Sardar Patel University, Mandi, as chief guest, and Dr Desh Bandhu, president, SDP Sabha, New Delhi, as guest of honour.The valedictory session and award ceremony were graced by Ashish Butail, Member of Legislative Assembly, Palampur, and former Chief Parliamentary Secretary (Higher Education), Government of Himachal Pradesh, as chief guest, with Prof H R Sharma, former Pro Vice-Chancellor, Central University of Himachal Pradesh, and Dr Desh Bandhu.Dr Samar Dev Singh Charak also chaired the technical session on "Advancing Internal and External Quality Assurance in Higher Education Institutions", in which experts shared their experience of external quality assurance and institutional evaluation.Dr Charak dedicated the award of achievement to the students and faculty and said that the recognition truly belongs to them. He mentioned that the award reflects years of sustained effort in teaching, learning and community engagement, guided by the Trust's motto, "Knowledge for Liberation", and that it will inspire the institution to keep raising the standard of higher education in Jammu.

headline: NEWS RECEIVED FROM PB BJP PRINT MEDIA AT CHANDIGARH
content: Zero Announcements and Endless Jokes: Kejriwal and Mann Dodged All Five Questions on Moga Stage: Anil Sarin Chief Minister reduced a purported five-year report card rally to stand-up comedy with not a single concrete announcement for farmers, youth, employees, or industry Diverting 2,960 public buses and splurging taxpayers' money cannot hide five years of misrule; Punjabis will teach AAP a Delhi-style lesson in 2027 Chandigarh, November 26-Telling jokes from a political stage with zero concrete announcements will not make Punjab khushhaal (prosperous), Punjab BJP general secretary Anil Sarin said today, slamming Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and AAP National Convenor Arvind Kejriwal for reducing the Aam Aadmi Party’s Moga rally to hollow theatrics while dodging every single one of the five direct questions posed by the BJP on their five-year governance record. Reacting sharply to the speeches at the ‘Khushhaal Punjab Maha Rally’ in Moga, Sarin remarked that when people brought in from across the state on commandeered government buses expected substantive policy announcements and answers on their daily hardships, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann once again resorted to cracking jokes and delivering scripted punchlines. "Punjab is bleeding from drug overdoses, extortion calls, and mounting debt, yet the Chief Minister treats governance like a comedy stage. Neither Kejriwal nor Mann made a single meaningful announcement for farmers, unemployed youth, government employees, or traders. Jokes and stand-up routines do not wipe a mother's tears, clear pending dues, or make Punjab prosperous," Sarin stated. Pointing out that both Arvind Kejriwal and Bhagwant Mann maintained complete silence on the BJP's five-point chargesheet, the Punjab BJP general secretary said their evasion itself is an admission of guilt across every front:

headline: Pending repairs delay Rose Club reopening
content: Chandigarh: Chandigarh’s Rose Club in Sector 16 missed its scheduled Nov reopening after the private contractor failed to finish repair and infrastructure upgrades within the six-month deadline, seeking a three-month extension from the MC despite having deposited the requisite fee.Allotted on a 10-year public-private partnership (PPP) model—a first for the MC—at the highest annual concession fee of Rs 26.76 lakh, the tender was approved by the MC General House over six months ago. Under the agreement, the contractor was required to complete upgrades as per laid-down norms and make the club operational by Nov.“Since the building is located in a heritage Grade-I area of the city, major demolition and construction were not allowed. To convert the Rose Club into a proper dining area, restaurant, and other required spaces, the authority permitted interior repairs and infrastructure upgrades without touching or altering the outer structure. Though the contractor has completed the majority of the work, a few tasks remain pending, for which he has sought a few more months. Besides operation and maintenance, the agency will ensure proper structural safety and upkeep of the building,” sources told TOI.Once operational, the agency will offer a restaurant, café, gaming zone, library, gymnasium, and indoor and outdoor games, alongside club memberships and social events—excluding weddings—while preserving the premises’ cultural integrity.Under the contract terms, the MC handed over the club on an “as-is-where-is” basis and is assisting the agency in securing utilities. Existing power and water connections are to be discontinued, with the contractor required to apply for fresh connections within one month of receiving the letter of acceptance (LOA).To ensure compliance with civic and environmental norms, the MC will constitute a designated project monitoring committee to oversee the concessionaire’s performance. Additionally, the civic body may authorise an officer to monitor activities and conduct surprise inspections for violations at any time, while leaving all other spaces available for the agency’s use.Agency’s key obligationsThe concessionaire must obtain all mandatory clearances, including fire safety, food, and bar licences, for smooth operations. It is also required to enter into annual maintenance contracts (AMCs) with vendors for various installations at its own cost.Further, the agency must maintain the entire premises in accordance with good industry practices, uphold strict hygiene—bearing any penalties imposed for insanitation—and comply with all noise, air, and water pollution regulations.

headline: Lalu’s claim of political conspiracy exposed by Delhi HC order: BJP
content: Patna, Nov 26 (PTI) The BJP in Bihar on Thursday said the Delhi High Court’s decision to uphold the framing of charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad and his family in the IRCTC scam case had exposed the RJD president’s allegations of a “political conspiracy”. In a statement, state BJP spokesperson Neeraj Kumar Sharma accused Prasad of indulging in “crony capitalism” during his tenure at the Centre and promoting “jungle raj” when the RJD was in power in Bihar. “The BJP stands for the rule of law and eradication of corruption. The Delhi High Court order has made it clear that the judiciary has rejected Lalu Prasad’s claim of political conspiracy,” Sharma said. The Delhi High Court upheld a trial court’s decision to frame charges against Prasad, his wife Rabri Devi, who succeeded him as Bihar chief minister, their younger son and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, and other accused named in the CBI charge sheet. Sharma said the trial court had ordered the framing of charges against the accused under relevant provisions of the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act. “Bihar has suffered a lot on account of jungle raj. It is time for the Lalu family to be brought to justice,” he said.

headline: Who will build a sustainable Delhi-NCR? India's civil engineering talent crisis
content: Ask a school student what they want to study and the answer is almost always computers, AI or data science. Few say physics, geology or civil engineering. That quiet preference is becoming a national problem, and Delhi-NCR is where it shows: a Rs 1,635 crore flyover that jammed within a day of opening in September 2026, metro stations that do not connect, and a landmark bridge that went seven years without a structural check. India has never lacked builders. It now risks lacking enough people who are trained, rewarded and empowered to build sustainably, maintain wisely and plan for the long term. Only strong public policy can change that trajectory.A sustainable engineering legacyIndia's engineers practised sustainability long before the word existed. The reservoirs of Dholavira and the covered drains of Mohenjo-daro (c. 2500 BCE) were designed around water security, sanitation and climate. The Kallanai (Grand Anicut), built nearly 2,000 years ago, still irrigates the Cauvery delta.Medieval builders turned stone into lasting infrastructure. Thanjavur's Brihadeeswara Temple (1010 CE) rises about 66 m on interlocking granite, while Konark, Khajuraho and Madurai's Meenakshi show mastery of load and craft. Stepwells, Rajasthan's forts and Lucknow's Bara Imambara (1784), whose vast central hall spans without pillars or beams, were built to last centuries. The colonial era added canals, railways and institutions: Thomason College (1847), now IIT Roorkee, designed the Solani Aqueduct for the Upper Ganga Canal, and Lutyens' New Delhi and Kolkata's Howrah Bridge followed.The ambition endures even today. The 9 km Atal Tunnel opened year-round Himalayan access, the Chenab Bridge is the world's highest railway arch bridge, the New Pamban Bridge is India's first vertical-lift rail sea bridge, and the Statue of Unity stands 182 m tall. Union Budget 2026-27 raises public capital spending to Rs 12.2 lakh crore from Rs 11.2 lakh crore. Yet money alone does not make good infrastructure.The computer science boom and the neglect of foundationsThe imbalance begins in the classroom. In JEE Advanced 2026, 365 of the top 500 rankers chose computer science; only two chose civil engineering. Engineering enrolments rose from 53.73% in 2020-21 to 75.07% in 2024-25, driven overwhelmingly by computing, while 409 B.Tech civil engineering programmes closed between 2012-13 and 2024-25.Basic sciences are failing more quietly. Nearly a dozen PhD fellows at IITs and IISERs reported going three to nine months without stipends, and most said they would prefer fellowships abroad. The Vigyan Dhara budget fell 22%, from Rs 1,827 crore to Rs 1,425 crore, and about 70% of the Department of Science and Technology's budget goes to interest-free loans for private firms in areas such as semiconductors.Students are responding rationally. Computer science offers higher starting salaries, remote work and predictable growth; civil engineering offers demanding site work, regulatory hurdles and slower progression. Yet geology, hydrology, materials science, structural engineering and mathematics are the foundation on which every road, bridge and water system stands. India faces an "app-to-asphalt gap": a generation skilled at optimising digital platforms but increasingly distant from designing the roads, bridges, water systems and cities society depends on.Why projects fail: From Bhopal to BarapullahIndia's infrastructure failures are rarely about funding. They reflect poor planning, fragmented governance, weak accountability and neglected maintenance. In Bhopal, a Rs 18 crore rail overbridge with an almost 90-degree turn led to disciplinary action against engineers and the blacklisting of firms. The 2022 Morbi bridge collapse in Gujarat killed 135 people. In Nagpur, the Rs 998 crore Indora-Dighori flyover drew criticism when its alignment placed it above a residential balcony. Delhi-NCR offers five lessons at closer range.Barapullah phase III, Delhi. Approved in 2014 and due in 2017, the Rs 1,635 crore corridor opened in September 2026. Six lanes of merging traffic funnel into three, and a loop near Sundial Park ends at a sharp angle. Diversions from NH-24 and the DND Flyway added to the jams. Infrastructure must be designed as part of a network, not as an isolated structure.RTR flyover, Vasant Vihar. The 900 m single-carriageway flyover, opened around 2009, could not handle roughly 2 lakh vehicles a day. Its 2.7 km, three-lane replacement, begun in November 2014, missed seven deadlines and was finished in June 2019 after residents fought over a service lane in court. The first design was outgrown within a decade.Signature bridge, Wazirabad. Opened in 2018 at about Rs 1,518 crore, the cable-stayed landmark had no structural assessment for seven years. Upkeep passed from the tourism corporation to the PWD amid budget limits, and in 2026 the PWD sought a consultant and IIT Delhi and Kanpur teams. Early checks flagged damaged road surfaces and railings, and videos of the bridge swaying in wind raised questions about its wind-resistance testing. We fund icons but not upkeep.Noida sectors 51/52. The Aqua Line's Sector 51 and the Blue Line's Sector 52 stations are 430 m apart, so passengers walk and clear ticketing and security twice. NMRC conceded in December 2023 that even a footbridge with travellators would not solve it and re-aligned the Aqua Line extension. Separate agencies planned separate lines, not one journey.Bhangel elevated road, Noida. The 5.5 km road began with a Rs 468 crore budget, and a request for Rs 150 crore more was rejected. Its deadline slid from December 2022 to December 2023, partly because the design changed from two to four entry-exit loops, while congestion grew. Another afterthought loop is now being designed for the 7X sectors.The root causes repeat: design in silos, lowest-bid contracting, no liable engineer or independent audit, and neglected maintenance.Technology alone is not the solutionIndia is investing heavily in emerging technology through the Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF). These matter, but innovation policy increasingly leans toward semiconductors, electronics, AI and software. Equal attention is due to construction technology, structural monitoring, climate resilience, advanced materials, urban drainage and water management. Infrastructure is the platform on which every digital economy rests.Sustainability: Relearning what earlier builders knewHistoric builders designed for climate, geography and durability. A sustainable strategy must move beyond lowest-cost construction and focus on long-term performance. That means designing major public assets for a 100-year life, judging projects on lifecycle cost rather than upfront spend, building in resilience to floods, extreme heat, storms and groundwater stress, and counting the carbon footprint of materials. Sustainable infrastructure is not an environmental luxury. It is an economic necessity that cuts maintenance costs, lowers emissions and strengthens resilience across generations.What the government must doOne NCR infrastructure authority spanning Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan agencies, so roads and metro are planned as one journey.A public "durability passport" for every government asset, listing design life, materials and audit dates.Audit before opening independent design review, traffic simulation, a soft launch and a named engineer of record.Fund upkeep ring-fenced maintenance budgets and five-yearly inspections.Fix incentives for basic science extend RDI, ANRF and fellowships to geoscience, hydrology, materials and construction technology, and pay stipends on time.Make civil worth choosing competitive starting pay, chartered-engineer licensing, and Civil-plus-Computing degrees with site internships, with IIT Delhi and other NCR institutes as design reviewers.Delhi-NCR is the showcase of India's infrastructure ambition. If the government makes building, and the science beneath it, a career worth choosing, our coders can help build the next marvel, not just the app to find it.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

headline: CIMMYT–BISA Inaugurates New Office at NASC Complex, New Delhi, Strengthens Longstanding Partnership with ICAR
content: The new office of the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT) and the Borlaug Institute for South Asia (BISA) was inaugurated at NASC, New Delhi, in the presence of Dr Bram Govaerts, Director General, CIMMYT and BISA, and Dr M. L. Jat, Secretary, DARE and Director General, ICAR. The inaugural ceremony was attended by Dr B. M. Prasanna, Managing Director, BISA and CIMMYT Regional Director for Asia; Dr Mahesh K. Gathala, CIMMYT Country Representative for India; and senior dignitaries from ICAR, including Mr Gyanendra Tripathi, Additional Secretary, DARE and Secretary, ICAR; Dr J. K. Jena, Deputy Director General (Fisheries Science); Dr Rajbir Singh, Deputy Director General (Agricultural Extension); and Dr Naveen Singh, Assistant Director General (International Relations). Mr Narmadeswar Lal, Principal Secretary (Agriculture), Government of Bihar; Dr B. S. Dhillon, Former Vice-Chancellor, Punjab Agricultural University; and representatives from various CGIAR centres were also present. The ceremony commenced with a ribbon-cutting and ceremonial lighting of the lamp, followed by the unveiling of the inaugural plaque by Dr M. L. Jat and Dr Bram Govaerts. Addressing the CIMMYT–BISA staff, the two leaders reflected on the longstanding partnership between ICAR and CIMMYT, spanning more than six decades, and its significant contribution to agricultural research, innovation and food security in India and South Asia. They emphasized the importance of reinvigorating this collaboration in the coming years to address emerging agricultural challenges and advance sustainable agricultural development. The inauguration reaffirmed the shared commitment of the partner institutions to strengthening collaborative research and promoting productive, inclusive, sustainable and resilient agri-food systems. The new office marks an important milestone in the continued partnership between ICAR, CIMMYT and BISA, providing further impetus to scientific collaboration, agricultural innovation and research-led development.

headline: Lookout Circular issued against CJP’s Saurav Das, Centre tells Delhi HC
content: New Delhi: The Centre on Thursday informed the Delhi High Court that a Look Out Circular has been issued by the Mumbai Police against CJP co-convener Saurav Das, who was stopped at the airport from travelling to the United Kingdom. The submission was made before Justice Amit Mahajan, who issued notice and sought a response from the Centre on Das’s plea challenging the government’s move to stop him from travelling. The court listed the matter for further hearing on December 9. During the hearing, the Centre’s counsel said a Look Out Circular (LOC) was issued against Das by the Mumbai Police on November 23 and that a show-cause notice was also issued to him and he is yet to respond to it. Das’s counsel submitted that he was not made aware of any LOC, the reason for its issuance and its purpose. The court was hearing a plea by Das, who was stopped from flying to the United Kingdom for an event at Oxford University, where he was slated to speak on the “cockroach movement”.

headline: Repeat offender arrested for sexually assaulting 10-year-old girl in northwest Delhi park: Police
content: A recently released repeat offender was arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting a 10-year-old girl inside a park in northwest Delhi on Tuesday evening, police said.Police officers said Rajesh, who was arrested in a similar case involving a minor in north Delhi in 2018 and was later convicted, had recently been released from jail. He was in the park when he allegedly spotted the girl.The girl, a Class 4 student at a private school in Delhi, was on her way to her uncle’s house when she stopped at the park, where the incident took place, officers said.“As per the girl, she was inside the park playing when the accused came and dragged her towards a corner. He attempted to rape her when she started screaming and the public nearby heard her. They all rushed to help her. They caught the accused and assaulted him. They also made a PCR call,” a senior police officer said.A case was registered under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, police said.Police said Rajesh was arrested in a similar case of sexual assault on a minor in Roop Nagar in 2018 and was subsequently convicted and sent to prison.“He was recently released from jail and again went on to target a minor. The public saved the minor and caught the accused in time,” another officer said.

headline: Delhi, UP redesign drain to send 200 cusecs of treated water into Yamuna’s most polluted stretch
content: The Yamuna’s winter froth problem along the Kalindi Kunj-Asgarpur stretch could see some improvement, with the Delhi and Uttar Pradesh governments undertaking work to channel more than 200 cusecs of treated wastewater into the river through a redesigned Abul Fazal drain.A senior government official said work is underway on a 2.8-km-long, over 27-foot-wide drain to carry treated water from the Okhla sewage treatment plant (STP) downstream of the Okhla Barrage, in a bid to improve the river’s environmental flow and dilute pollutants.The remodelling and desilting of the Abul Fazal drain is being carried out by the Uttar Pradesh irrigation department with funding from the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG), the official added.Also Read:Yamuna toxic foam: Why is the river covered with glacier-like layers of froth?Once completed, the drain will be among the widest in Delhi, comparable in scale to the Najafgarh drain. Wastewater from more than a dozen residential areas, including Shaheen Bagh, Zakir Nagar, Noor Nagar, Okhla Vihar, Jamia Nagar, Jasola Village and Abul Fazal Enclave, will be diverted to the Okhla STP for treatment before being discharged into the Yamuna downstream of the barrage, an official said.The project is expected to improve the river’s environmental flow and dilute pollutants in the stretch that falls under Uttar Pradesh’s jurisdiction, the official added.Also Read: Delhi govt begins Yamuna defoaming work, clears ₹91L for froth studyA second official said untreated wastewater entering the Okhla stretch of the Yamuna was heavily polluted. When the water falls from the barrage, the resulting turbulence contributes to foam formation.The problem becomes particularly severe around Kalindi Kunj between October and December, coinciding with the Chhath Puja festival. The froth on the river during this period has often become a subject of political debate.The ongoing work on the Abul Fazal drain is aimed at addressing the problem by ensuring that treated wastewater, rather than untreated sewage, enters the river. The Delhi government has provided approximately ₹14 crore for the redesign. Once the work is completed, the drain is expected to carry more than 200 cusecs of treated water into the Yamuna, the official said.

headline: Saurav Das not allowed to travel abroad as Mumbai Police issued LOC against him: Centre tells Delhi High Court
content: The Centre on Thursday told Delhi High Court that Cockroach Janta Party co-convener Saurav Das was stopped at the Indira Gandhi airport as the Mumbai Police had issued a lookout circular against him, which prevented him from travelling abroad. The submission was made before Justice Amit Mahajan, who sought a reply from the government to Das' plea against the refusal to allow him to travel abroad. The HC was hearing Das's plea challenging the government authorities' decision to stop him from flying abroad.The matter will be heard next on December 9..CJP's Saurav Das issued show cause notice by Chennai passport authorities, asked to clarify place of birth .During the hearing, the Centre's counsel said a request was made by the Maharashtra Police to open an LOC against Das, and it was issued on the intervening night of November 22-23.Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma and standing counsel Ashish Dixit, representing the Centre, said a show-cause notice was also issued to Das on November 23, and he is yet to respond to it.On Monday, Das was prevented from boarding a Lond-bound flight over alleged discrepancies in his passport details. He was travelling to attend engagements at various UK universities to speak about the 'Cockroach Movement' scheduled between November 24 and December 1, organised by the London School of Economics Amnesty Society, the Student Federation of India at the University of Edinburgh, the Cambridge South Asia Forum at the University of Cambridge and the Oxford Union.According to reports, Das' passport has been issued in Chennai in 2019, with the city listed as his birthplace, although he was reportedly born in Delhi. The passport office issued him a show-cause notice, giving him seven days to explain the discrepancy and advising him against international travel.Das has alleged that the notice was issued to prevent his travel due to his involvement in political activism. In his plea, Das has stated that the show cause notice was issued to him by the passport authorities on Monday seeking clarification regarding his place of birth. (With PTI inputs)

headline: Triple threat to lungs: Delhi NCR doctors see rise in chest tightness, dry cough
content: Delhi-NCR's winter air is becoming a concern for people who are already struggling with cough, wheezing and breathing discomfort. Hospitals are seeing patients with breathing issues as falling temperatures coincide with poor air quality and seasonal flu infections.The wider impact of lung disease in the capital is also reflected in a recent RTI investigation by PTI Bhasha. Data obtained from AIIMS, Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and the Delhi State Cancer Institute showed that 6,581 lung cancer cases were recorded across three of these hospitals between January 2020 and July 2026. The four hospitals together reported 913 deaths linked to lung cancer during the period, roughly one death every three days.The problem is not just the visible layer of smog. Fine particulate matter, winter viruses and allergens can make symptoms harder to manage. This overlap is leading to more people seeking medical attention for symptoms that may initially seem like a routine seasonal cough.Dr. Mayank Saxena, Director and Unit Head of Interventional Pulmonology and Pulmonary Intensive Care at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Noida, says doctors are commonly seeing patients with constant dry cough, wheezing and chest tightness. He describes the situation as a threefold problem involving winter temperatures, deteriorating air quality and seasonal flu.What are the most common respiratory symptoms doctors are observing in OPDs these days?Dr. Mayank Saxena: We usually see a long queue of people suffering from constant dry cough, wheezing and feeling of chest tightness in OPD . The underlying reason for these ailments involves a threefold problem of dropping temperatures in winter, bad air quality index and seasonal flu. The poisonous smog traps different allergens and viruses and makes the inflammation of the airways more pronounced.How is the current rise in air pollution affecting lung health, particularly among children, elderly people?Dr. Mayank Saxena: Pollution by fine particulate matter (PM2.5) eludes the body's natural protective mechanisms and leads to extensive alveolar inflammation. In children, it slows down lung growth and leads to recurring infections. In the elderly and patients suffering from asthma or COPD, these contaminants cause serious acute episodes and routinely lead to hospitalization or even require intensive pulmonary management.What precautions should people take to protect their respiratory health during this season, and when should symptoms like persistent cough or breathing difficulty not be ignored?Dr. Mayank Saxena: Keep yourself safe by using N95 masks in open air, HEPA air purifiers and taking yearly flu or pneumococcal vaccinations. Never take lightly a cough lasting more than two weeks, blood-stained expectoration, noisy respiration and shortness of breath while at rest. Any of these indications signals the need for doctor's intervention to prevent damaging lungs irreversibly.With winter pollution and seasonal infections occurring together, respiratory symptoms should not be dismissed as a routine part of the season. A cough that continues for days, repeated episodes of wheezing or a feeling of tightness in the chest may indicate that the airways are under considerable stress. For people with asthma and COPD, exposure to polluted air can trigger sudden flare-ups and make existing symptoms more difficult to control. Children and older adults also need particular attention because prolonged exposure to fine particles can affect lung health and increase the risk of respiratory infections.As pollution levels remain a concern across Delhi-NCR, recognising symptoms early and reducing exposure can help prevent respiratory problems from becoming more serious.

headline: FIR in Delhi over comedian's 'objectionable' remarks against Chhath Puja
content: The Delhi Police has registered an FIR at south Delhi's Saket police station over an alleged objectionable video involving remarks against women from Bihar and the religious and cultural traditions associated with Chhath Puja. The FIR was registered after a complaint against the stand-up comedy event, which named performer Yash Maheshwari. The complaint alleged that objectionable remarks were made during a programme held at the Saket-based comedy club on October 24. The complainant has sought examination of video recordings, social media posts and other digital evidence. The FIR, which does not mention the comedian's name, has been registered under Sections 79 (word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman), 196 (promoting enmity between different groups on ground of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony), 296 (obscene acts and songs) and 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace) of the BNS.

headline: Delhi AQI today: India’s capital suffers from severe air quality at 263 on November 26, faces high risk of asthma
content: Smoky haze covered Delhi on Thursday, November 26, as air quality reached the severe category. The Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 263 at 8:41 AM on the US scale. It fell 71 points from the overnight peak of 334. New Delhi ranked 60th among the world’s most polluted cities at the time.Delhi’s air quality improved through Wednesday afternoon before worsening again in the evening. The AQI fell to 165 at 5:01 PM, its lowest in the previous 24 hours. It rose above 300 before midnight, reaching 334 at 3:31 AM on Thursday. Readings remained above 300 until after 5 AM, then eased later in the morning.The November calendar shows a reading of 226 for Wednesday, down from 236 on Tuesday. Monday’s reading was higher at 311. The highest daily figure through November 25 was 666 on November 9. The next highest was 547 on November 12. All 14 days in the first fortnight had readings above 300.Delhi’s seven-day AQI peaked at 532 at 6 AM on November 19. That seven-day period ended on November 25. The lowest reading in that series was 186 at noon on November 25. Early morning readings were above 400 on several days during that stretch. The latest morning reading was roughly half the seven-day peak.Delhi’s PM10 level was 261 micrograms per cubic metre across the city at 8:41 am. The World Health Organization’s guideline is 45 micrograms per cubic metre.Delhi’s reading was about 5.8 times that level. The PM10 reading fell in the unhealthy category. The concentration of finer PM2.5 particles was 186 micrograms per cubic metre.Carbon monoxide stood at 2,214 parts per billion. Nitrogen dioxide measured 20 parts per billion while sulphur dioxide measured six. Ozone was recorded at one part per billion. The temperature was 17°C and humidity was 48%. The wind speed was 5.4 km/h, and the UV index was 0.5.New Delhi had the highest AQI among 8 Indian metros. It ranked 273rd in that comparison, followed by Kolkata at 256. Pune recorded 198, Mumbai 185 and Ahmedabad 175. Chennai stood at 125. Bengaluru had the lowest reading at 71, followed by Hyderabad at 92.High risk of asthmaAQI.in flagged a high risk of asthma symptoms at the reported pollution level. The symptoms listed include wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness and a persistent cough.It advised people with asthma to stay indoors and keep windows closed to reduce exposure. It also advised against strenuous outdoor activity and exposure to secondhand smoke.

headline: Delhi auto-taxi unions meet CM, seek fare hike, EV policy review and action on bike taxis | Hindustan Times
content: Representatives of Delhi's auto-rickshaw and taxi unions met Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Wednesday to press for a fare revision and action on several issues affecting drivers, including the operation of illegal bike taxis and the fitness testing system.Fare revision and bike taxi operationsThe delegation requested an increase in auto and taxi fares, citing the rise in compressed natural gas (CNG) prices. The unions also called for action against privately registered motorcycles allegedly being used commercially as taxis without authorisation."In light of rising CNG prices, the union urged the Delhi government to increase the fares for auto and taxi services. The union has also demanded a ban on the widespread, illegal operation of private-registered motorcycles being used as taxis in Delhi," a statement from Delhi Auto Rickshaw Sangh said.The meeting follows a protest held earlier this month at Ramlila Maidan by the Delhi Auto Rickshaw Sangh and Pradesh Taxi Union, both affiliated to the Bhartiya Majdoor Sangh. The unions had raised concerns over driver-related issues during the demonstration.Demand to roll back fitness testing systemThe delegation also asked the Delhi government to withdraw the Automated Testing Station fitness system. Delhi Auto Rickshaw Centre General Secretary Rajendra Soni said Gupta had assured the representatives that their concerns would be taken up with the relevant departments."The delegation urged the chief minister to roll back the Automated Testing Station fitness system. The chief minister assured us that she will hold a meeting with all the concerned officials and would consider all our legitimate demands and take steps at the earliest to provide relief to drivers," Soni said.Welfare board and EV policy reviewAnother key demand concerned the formation of a welfare board for auto and taxi drivers in Delhi. The unions said the government had committed to setting up the body, but the process had not moved forward despite more than 18 months having passed since it took office."More than a year and a half has passed since the government took office, but nothing has moved forward on this. The administration should take immediate action to form this welfare board for Delhi's auto and taxi drivers," the statement added.The delegation also sought a review of Delhi's electric vehicle (EV) policy, with the unions asking the government to consider drivers' interests while reassessing its provisions. They further called for faster processing of drivers' applications and documentation at the Delhi Transport Department.(With inputs from PTI)

headline: Delhi salon owner held for running shell firm, providing bank account to cybercriminals
content: A Delhi-based salon owner was arrested on Wednesday for allegedly operating a shell firm and providing cybercriminals with a current bank account linked to the firm to dupe a person in Faridabad, police said on Thursday.Police said the account was opened on the basis of the firm in which ₹2 lakh out of ₹1.08 crore duped from a Faridabad resident was routed.The accused was identified as Mohammad Shahwez, a resident of South Delhi. He was arrested by a team of the Cybercrime (NIT) police station.Police said 84 other complaints from different states had been registered against the bank account of the firm, Trident International, which belonged to Shahwez.A resident of Sector 21 in Faridabad was allegedly duped of ₹1.08 crore between September and November 2025 on the pretext of investing in the stock market, police said.The victim received a WhatsApp message from a person impersonating an employee of SBI Securities, who sent him a link to open a brokerage account.The victim was later added to a WhatsApp group and lured into investing in the stock market with promises of high returns, Yashpal Yadav, public relations officer of Faridabad Police, said.“Between September and November 2025, the complainant transferred a total of ₹1.08 crore to different bank accounts. He later realised that he had fallen victim to cyber fraud, following which a case was registered at the Cybercrime (NIT) police station,” he added.Yadav said that during the investigation, police found that ₹2 lakh of the defrauded amount had been transferred to the bank account of Trident International, of which Shahwez was the account holder.“The accused was produced before a court and remanded in police custody for two days for further interrogation,” he said, adding that this was the fourth arrest in the case.

headline: Two Delhi teens turn ordinary school fans into air purifiers with a Rs 140 filter; project reaches 20,000
content: In a city where pollution often makes its way indoors, a fan that circulates air does not necessarily circulate clean air. For children in schools that cannot afford air purifiers, that is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day in classrooms with little protection from fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which refers to airborne particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less.Two Delhi students, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle chose not to ask schools to buy expensive equipment. They asked whether the fans already fitted in classrooms could do more. The answer became Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed a filter which fits over an ordinary table or wall fan and costs approximately Rs 140."Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo told The Better India. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection."Working with the fan schools already haveThe main technical problem was building a filter that could trap PM2.5 without restricting the airflow of a regular fan. After testing different designs, the team settled on a balloon-shaped filter made from electret media, which uses electrostatically charged fibres to attract and capture tiny particles, they told The Better India.The filter sits over the fan with an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates it, which increases the surface area available for filtration. It needs no additional motor, no electrical modification and no specialised installation. It can be fitted in under a minute without tools.To develop and test the technology, the students emailed the India team of Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. The company supplied the media free of cost and worked with them on research and development. That support has kept the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter."The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it," the founders told The Better India. "By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure."The numbers behind the filterAffordability was only half the task. The students also had to show that the filter made a measurable difference.According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results. In a closed room of about 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly fell from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour, a reduction of over 90%.The results depend on room size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use.There is also a visible sign. "One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use," the founders told The Better India. They describe it as a reminder of how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms.From a pilot of 295 classrooms to 20,000 studentsConvincing schools to trust a product built by high school students was not easy. Many institutions were hesitant at first, and demonstrations of the testing behind the filters helped the team build confidence.Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and about 8,000 students. It has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics.Growth has come with delays. Identifying schools, securing permissions and moving through institutional processes have slowed several installations. "Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging," the duo told The Better India. "A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals."The work has earned recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his role in Project Vayu, though he credits Samarth and their collaborators for the initiative as a whole.Samarth, for his part, said that the project has taught him something about innovation. "It doesn't always require inventing something entirely new," he said. "Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible."The plan to reach more schools across IndiaThe duo now hopes to take Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and, eventually, other parts of India. They want to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help the filters reach children who need them.The belief behind it is simple: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend.If necessity is the mother of invention, this case shows that invention does not always need something new. Sometimes it needs someone to look at what is already in the room and ask what more it could do.Get the latest Education News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
